13060-the-persian-literature-comprising-:
Volume two of a 1900 anthology gathers four cornerstones of Persian letters in English dress, with an introduction by Richard J. H. Gottheil. It joins Firdausi's Shah Nameh, the Rubaiyat quatrains, a divan of lyric verse, and Saadi's Gulistan, or Rose Garden. Together they span epic history, love poetry, and moral prose from a long literary past.

Inside, kings and heroes face fate and pride, lovers plead and pine, and Saadi's short tales turn on patience, mercy, and the folly of anger. Some passages are missing, marked by lines of stars where the translator skipped ahead. Read as a whole, the volume shows how Persian writers mixed high romance with plain moral advice, and why these works traveled far beyond Persia.
22848-sandhya:
Dhan Gopal Mukerji published Sandhya, rendered here as Songs of Twilight, in 1917. The poems speak in a hushed, yearning voice. One addresses a tearful soul of laughter, untouched and unhurt, a born yet unborn presence, an undawning morning and a message still unbroken. Waiting runs through the lines like a refrain.

Mukerji wrote from inside two worlds, Indian by birth and American by residence. His verse blends devotion, nature, and longing in the manner of the Bengali poets he admired. Twilight suits his theme, the hour between day and dark, self and spirit. Readers new to his work will find short, musical pieces that ask to be read slowly and more than once.
41540-mga-paquigpulong-sa-iningles-ug-bi:
Mga Paquigpulong sa Iningles ug Binisaya is a phrase book for learning English through Cebuano, written by Gregorio de Santiago, an Augustinian friar, and printed at Manila in 1905. The title means conversations in English and Visayan. In his preface, in Cebuano, Santiago explains that the book began as dialogues he translated for the children he taught.

Encouraged by learned readers, he expanded those beginnings into a printed book, confessing its faults and asking the reader to look to its purpose: to open the road to speaking English. The lessons start with the English alphabet and the names of its letters, spelled out in Cebuano sounds. Santiago also warns that words differ in meaning between the towns of the Visayas. The book is a small monument of American-period Philippines: a friar teaching the new rulers' language out of his schoolroom dialogues.
42425-goya:
Goya is a colour art book on the Spanish painter who lived 1746 to 1826. The book stands in the Masterpieces in Colour set, edited by Roujon. Crastre wrote the French text, and Frederic Taber Cooper rendered it in English. Eight colour copies of the works stand through the small volume here. A portrait of Ferdinand Guillemardet from the Louvre fronts the plates.

Guillemardet was a high officer, half civil and half military in role. The First Republic sent such men to watch its armies and generals. Goya gave the head energy and high breeding in grey tones. One dash of brightness sits in the tricoloured scarf he wears. The life opens in 1760 with a monk on the Saragossa road. That monk walks from the convent of Santa Fé, book in hand. The boy Goya's world rises from that quiet Spanish morning scene.
42717-regulations-for-the-establishment-:
Regulations for the Establishment and Government of the Royal Military Asylum were printed in London in 1805 for Egerton at the Military Library, Whitehall. The asylum, founded under the Duke of York, housed and schooled the children of soldiers killed or serving abroad. This thin book is its first rule of life, from the commandant's duties down to the children's bread.

Hours, uniforms, lessons, punishments, and prayers stand in exact order. The school at Chelsea raised orphans of the Napoleonic wars to be soldiers, servants, and tradesmen in their turn. Rule books like this one show how the state first took charge of soldiers' children. Readers get a complete little code of charity and discipline from 1805.
49109-john-sherman-and-dhoya:
John Sherman and Dhoya pairs a short Irish novel with a tale, in a second edition printed in London. An apology signed Ganconagh opens the book, the pen name on the title matter. Part one sends John Sherman away from his home village of Ballah, and part two brings in Margaret Leland, the woman at the heart of his story.

Sherman revisits Ballah, meets a clergyman named William Howard, and at last returns for good. The tale Dhoya follows, a wilder piece of Irish legend and longing. The book is early work by a writer learning his craft, plain in scene yet full of poetry. Readers get a love story of exile and home, plus a glimpse of Irish myth.
50011-myths-and-folk-tales-of-the-russia:
Jeremiah Curtin gathered these myths and folk tales, published by Little, Brown at Boston in 1890. Curtin dedicates the book to Child, professor of English at Harvard University. His letter to Child recalls more than a quarter century of collecting myths, tales and ballads in all European languages.

That collection had grown under Child's hand to great size, Curtin writes in the dedication. The tales here come from Russians, western Slavs and Magyars in Curtin's translations. Curtin worked from the lips of storytellers in their own lands, and his versions keep the wonder, humor and cruelty of the originals for English readers.
50309-dave-dawson-in-libya:
Sidney Bowen wrote this war novel for young readers, with a copyright of nineteen forty-one. Dave Dawson flies for the Royal Air Force, and his pal Freddy Farmer rides behind him as gunner and observer. Their plane is a Blackburn Skua, part fighter and part dive bomber, working from a carrier in the Mediterranean Sea.

The boys scout ahead of the fleet, then take orders that send them toward Libya. Desert mystery, blazing sands, and a trap laid by a colonel fill the middle chapters. At one point the pair let themselves be taken prisoner on purpose. Later chapters bring lightning strikes by the air force and a last fight over the desert. The pace stays fast from patrol to finish.
73415-historical-record-of-the-eighty-se:
Historical Record of the Eighty Seventh Regiment is a part of a grand set of army records made by command of a king of Britain. The set aimed to give the history of each and every regiment in royal service. Its maker held a post at the Horse Guards in London, and the work came out by state leave.

A note on the print form of the text tells how slant text and notes are marked for the screen reader. A general order at the head, from the first day of a year in the eighteen thirties, states the kings will in the work. His aim, it says, was to do full justice to the deeds of his troops by a true record of each corps in turn.
britannica-1911-abu-l-atahiya:
Abu-l-'Atahiya (748-828) was an Arabian poet born at 'Ain ut-Tamar in the Hijaz, near Medina. His youth was spent in Kufa selling pottery, and he continued that trade after moving to Baghdad. Verse made him famous instead, above all poems addressed to 'Utba, a slave of the caliph al-Mahdi, who did not return his love.

Plainness is his claim on attention. Where poets of his day copied the old desert style, Abu-l-'Atahiya dropped the set qasida form and wrote fluently in many metres about common life and morals. Often pessimistic, he is counted among the earliest philosophic poets of the Arabs, and his later years turned ascetic.
britannica-1911-bismya:
Bismya is a group of ruin mounds in the Jezireh, nearer the Tigris than the Euphrates. The mounds run about a mile long, in low ridges nowhere over 40 feet high. They lie a day's journey south-east of Nippur, just below 32 degrees north. Excavations ran there for six months, from Christmas 1903 to June 1904. Dr Edgar J. Banks dug for the University of Chicago. The dig proved the mounds cover the ancient city of Adab, or Ud-Nun.

Adab was known before only from a mention in the Khammurabi code. A canal split the city, with the temple E-mach on an island between. Surface ruins belong to kings of Ur of the third millennium BC. Below them lay remains of Naram-Sin and Sargon, about 3000 BC. The prize finds were a white marble statue, Babylon's most ancient yet, and heaps of inlaid stone vases.
britannica-1911-chalukya:
Chalukya is the name of an Indian ruling house that held the Deccan in two long spells, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its rise and fall. The house ruled first from about 550 to 750, then again from 973 to 1190. The Chalukyas claimed to be Rajputs from the north who set their rule over the Dravidian folk of the tableland.

The line was founded by Pulakesin the First, who took Vatapi, now Badami, about 550. His grandson Pulakesin the Second made the house great. He set his brother as ruler in Vengi, and that branch split off as the Eastern Chalukyas. In 620 he beat Harsha, lord of the north, and fixed the Nerbudda river as the line between north and south. He also beat the Chola, Pandya and Kerala kings. In 642 a Pallava king took his capital and killed him, but his son restored the house.
britannica-1911-chandragupta-maurya:
Chandragupta Maurya is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chandragupta ruled India from 321 to 296 years before Christ. The Greeks knew him as Sandracottus. He founded the Maurya empire and was the first supreme ruler of India. He was a son of a king of Magadha by a woman of humble birth. As a youth he was driven into exile by a kinsman king.

The article tells how he met Alexander the Great during his wandering. He gathered a large force from the warlike clans of the northwest. After Alexander died he beat the Macedonian garrisons and took the Punjab. He then took Magadha and set himself on its throne. With a vast army he overran all northern India. In 305 he defeated Seleucus and forced a hard peace. He died about six years later, leaving the empire to his son.
britannica-1911-chupriya:
Chupriya was the chief town of the Morava district of Servia, on the rail line from Belgrade to Nish. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the right bank of the Morava river, which small sail boats could reach at that point. Its town count at the turn of the age was about six thousand souls.

The entry praises the fine cattle bred in the low lands round the town. It notes trade in plums and other farm goods, and a light rail line to coal pits through beech woods and hills. Near by towns weave cloth and hold markets. The piece ends with an old friary in the hills, its walls marked by shot, and a tale of Tsar Lazar, who chose a crown in heaven and fell in battle.
britannica-1911-garashanin-iliya:
Iliya Garashanin, a Serbian statesman born in eighteen twelve, was the son of a peasant. His father made money by sending cattle and pigs to Austria for sale. By skill and wealth that father won some weight in the country. He sought the best schooling he could give his son in Hungary. The boy learned in a Greek school, then in a German one.

Gifted and well trained, the young Iliya came to the front very quickly. In eighteen thirty six Prince Milosh made him a colonel over the new regular army. In eighteen forty two he became aide to the home minister of Serbia. From then until eighteen sixty seven he held home office again and again. His rule there was marked by energy and by justice. Greater still were his services as minister for foreign affairs.
britannica-1911-gaya:
Gaya is a city and district of British India, in the Patna division of Bengal, 85 miles south of Patna by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the city 71,288 people in 1901. It falls into two parts: Gaya proper, home of the priests, and Sahibganj, the business quarter with the civil offices.

The city's sanctity comes from events in Buddha's life, retold through a local legend of the demon Gaya, pinned under a stone by the gods. Vishnu promised that pilgrims to the spot would escape the Hindu place of torment. Forty-five sacred spots lie in and around the city, the temple of Vishnupada chief among them, drawing thousands of pilgrims each year. The entry then surveys the district, 4,712 square miles of level plain with wooded hills along its southern edge.
britannica-1911-goya:
Goya in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is a short place entry, not the life of the Spanish painter. It describes a river town and port in Corrientes province in Argentina. The town serves as the trade centre for the south west part of the province. It is also the chief town of a district with the same name.

The entry places the town on a side channel of the Parana river, on low ground that floods in wet weather. It notes broad streets, a parish church, and a national school. Local farms raise cattle and grow oranges for export. A short note traces the town back to the year eighteen hundred and seven.
britannica-1911-hasbeya:
Hasbeya, a town of the Druses about thirty six miles west of Damascus, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits at the foot of Mount Hermon in Syria. The town looks over a deep bowl of land from which a brook flows to the Hasbani. Its people number about 5000, of whom 4000 are Christians.

Both sides of the valley are planted in terraces with olives, vines, and other fruit trees. Grapes there are dried or made into a kind of syrup for use. An American Protestant mission took root in the town in 1846. That small flock met much hardship at first from the Greek Church, then from the Druses. In 1860 near one thousand Christians were massacred there, while others fled to Tyre or Sidon. Crusaders once held its castle, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-kenya:
Kenya is a great volcanic mountain in British East Africa, set just south of the equator. It is one of the highest mountains of Africa, its top peak reaching 17,007 feet, with a possible error of 30 feet either way. The central core, a set of steep pyramids, is the core of a much worn old volcano. When its crater was whole it may have stood 2000 feet higher.

Lavas dip away in all directions from the central core, pointing to one single volcanic mass. Ridges run out from the central peaks and are split by broad valleys that end upward in vast cirques. The most weighty ridge centres in the peak Lenana, 16,300 feet high, at the eastern end of the central group. Through that peak runs the chief watershed of the mountain, in a general line from north to south.
britannica-1911-kshattriya:
The Kshattriya form one of the four first castes of India, the others being the Brahman, the Vaisya and the Sudra. They were the warrior caste. Their task was to protect the people, and they were bound to hold back from sensual pleasures.

When the Brahmans rose to the top, the Kshattriyas were pressed down. Their revolt in answer gave birth to Buddhism and Jainism, and the founders of both faiths came from this caste. By tradition Parasurama wiped the Kshattriyas out, yet the rank is still granted to the modern Rajputs, and to the ruling families of the native states.
britannica-1911-legya:
Legya, called Lai-hka by the Shans, was a state in the southern Shan States of Burma, described in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covered 1,433 square miles, a rolling plateau at a bit under 3,000 feet. Its people fell sharply after civil war broke out, then rose again to 25,811 by 1901.

The entry says about seven-ninths of the farmed land grew wet rice, with upland rice, cotton, sugar-cane, and garden crops besides. Large orange groves had lately been planted in the west. The capital, Laihka, was noted for iron-work made from local iron, and lacquer-ware and pottery were also chief exports.
britannica-1911-maya:
The 1911 Britannica article on the Maya describes a great people of American Indians. They were the ruling race of Yucatan at the time of the Spanish conquest. Their lands covered parts of Mexico and Central America. They were divided into many nations. The Maya proper were chief among them. Others included the Huastecs, the Tzental, and the Quiché.

The article says their culture rivalled that of the Aztecs. Their traditions place their origin in the far north. They seem to have reached Yucatan by the fifth century. They were already in decline when the Spaniards arrived. Still, they resisted fiercely. They still form the bulk of the people of Yucatan. The article points readers elsewhere for their ruined cities.
britannica-1911-novaya-zemlya:
Novaya Zemlya is a land study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Arctic land off the north coast of Russia. The name means new land. Two large islands form the land, split by a narrow, winding channel. The whole chain runs near six hundred miles in a long curve.

The article places the land between the Barents Sea and the Kara Sea. It covers about 36,000 square miles of ground. Fjords and bays cut both coasts, more so on the west. Hills run through the whole land, with snow fields and ice sheets in the north. Near the strait the hills rise to 4,000 feet and more. Little was known of the deep interior at that time.
britannica-1911-sadiya:
Sadiya is the far north east border post of British India, in a district of Assam. It stands high on a grass plain, near ringed by forest clad hills. It sits on the right bank of a stream held to be the main flow of a great river. A rail line on the far bank links it to the main lines of the region.

The post is held by bands of native foot troops and armed police, the entry says. It forms the base of a chain of out posts on the border. A market sits there where hill men bring down goods to swap. Rubber, wax, ivory, and musk change hands for cloth, salt, and wares of metal.
britannica-1911-surabaya:
Surabaya is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a seaport of Java. The town stands in the eastern division of the island, on the narrow strait that separates Madura from Java, at the mouth of the Kali Mas river. Its population is given as 146,944, including 8,906 Europeans and 13,035 Chinese. The article calls it the principal trading town of Java.

The piece describes the port and its quarters. The roadstead is sheltered by Madura, and the town has important dockyards. It is also the headquarters of the military authorities for East Java, with artillery workshops. Railways running north-west, south-west and south link it with the whole island. The old town, inside its partly demolished walls, packs houses, shops and warehouses along narrow streets. The article judges the outlying quarters, such as Simpang with the government house, better places to live.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-ruiz-:
Lima-born Jesuit Antonio Ruiz de Montoya, who lived from 1585 to 1652, ranks among the most distinguished pioneers of Paraguay's original Jesuit mission and a remarkable linguist. After a wild youth he entered the Society of Jesus in 1606 and sailed that year with Father Diego Torres, first provincial of Paraguay, where he laboured for thirty years. The article paints a missionary of iron endurance, burning zeal, few wants, and great power of work.

With Fathers Cataldino and Mazeta he established the reductions of Guayra, settled mission towns that gathered wild tribes into church life, and is said to have baptized 100,000 Indians himself. As head of the missions from 1620 he oversaw reductions along the Paraná, Uruguay, and Tape rivers, adding thirteen to twenty-six already standing. When Brazilian slave hunters threatened Guayra, he helped plan the defence and removal of its people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-ruiz-de:
Diego Ruiz de Montoya was a Spanish Jesuit theologian born at Seville in 1562. He entered the Jesuits in 1572, taking final vows two decades later. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his teaching of philosophy at Granada and theology for some twenty years at Cordova and Seville. He also served as rector of the College of Cordova and spoke for Andalusia at a general congregation.

His last years were given to writing, and friends praised his humility and integrity. When the Duke of Lerma offered to win papal leave to print his work on grace, Montoya refused to trade favors. Later writers ranked him among the most finished theologians of his age, joining historical learning to scholastic method.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MamantovIlya_Ma:
An FBI memorandum from June 1964 records a small appointment with large stakes. On June 4, 1964, at 10:10 in the morning, writer William Manchester met Director J. Edgar Hoover. Manchester had been chosen by Jacqueline Kennedy to write the authorized book on the assassination. His research required the bureau's cooperation.

The memo notes the meeting for the file, in the bureau's flat style. Behind it sits a tense relationship: a writer with the family's trust, an agency guarding its records, and a book that would be fought over before it appeared. The memorandum is one dated trace of that negotiation, preserved because the FBI wrote down even its courtesies.
podcast-dannyjones-B65mFXwqJYA:
A physicist who says he worked with NASA presents Danny Jones with a bold claim: antigravity has been cracked, and secret technology proves it. The guest says he can show evidence of craft and propulsion programs hidden from the public, built on physics the textbooks do not teach.

Jones asks for the proof and the guest walks through his material. Nothing in the episode meets the standard of published, repeatable science, and the claims should be heard as the guest's alone. The format is the appeal: a man with credentials making the strongest possible case for a hidden technological order. Listeners can enjoy the audacity while keeping their skepticism intact, a balance this series asks of its audience again and again. The recording is kept as the claim was made.
podcast-joerogan-22vmU-8LByA:
Musician Jason Everman tells one of rock's strangest life stories in this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Everman played guitar in Nirvana and bass in Soundgarden just before both bands broke huge. Instead of chasing fame after, he enlisted and became an Army Ranger and Special Forces soldier.

Everman walks through the grunge years, the tours, and why he walked away from that life. He explains what drew him to elite military service and the wars he fought in. Rogan, fascinated by the turn from stage lights to battlefield, draws out the details. Inspired listeners get a wild path told straight.
podcast-joerogan-kvitm0bMHyA:
Debunker Mick West brings his skeptic's toolkit to episode 959 of the Joe Rogan Experience. West runs Metabunk, where he tests famous claims with patient, hands-on analysis. He is the rare skeptic who explains footage frame by frame rather than mocking believers.

He and Rogan work through chemtrails, UFO videos, and the tricks of light and lens that fool the eye. Rogan defends his wilder guests while granting West his points. The episode is the skeptic's corner of the show at its fairest: a rational guest, heard in full, inside a studio famous for the opposite.
podcast-joerogan-l1jTUhwWJYA:
Eric Weinstein airs his grievance against Harvard in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, arguing that the university's power structure buried his work. Weinstein says his unified theory of physics was ignored and blocked by the academy he hoped would test it. The charge has powered his public career.

He tells Rogan how the snub unfolded and what it taught him about how science guards its gates. Rogan gives him the sympathetic hearing the journals, in Weinstein's telling, never did. The segment is the Geometric Unity saga in its personal form: one man's case against the house of modern physics.
podcast-joerogan-ywGTE_bobyA:
Comic Bryan Callen tells the story of his mushroom trip in this clip from Joe Rogan Experience episode 150. The segment comes from the show's young days, when Rogan's comic friends swapped drug stories freely. Callen, a stand-up and actor, delivers his tale for laughs and wonder.

Callen walks through the trip step by step, from the first strange feelings to the peak. He mixes fear, beauty, and pure comedy in the retelling. Rogan compares notes from his own psychedelic history and keeps the story rolling. Early fans will recognize the loose, funny spirit that built the show's first audience.
the-persian-literature-comprising-the-sh: Persian Literature, a revised edition of 1900 in two volumes, gathers the Shah Nameh, the Rubaiyat, the Divan, and the Gulistan. This second volume carries a special introduction by Richard J. H. Gottheil of Columbia University. Notes, a title page, and the start of a contents list are present; the poems and tales themselves are not. The contents shown are the Gulistan's chapters, from Of the Customs of Kings to Of the Impressions of Education.
